text: A support agent has four tools: `read_ticket`, `draft_reply`, `issue_refund`, and `delete_user_account`. Support staff only ever read tickets and draft replies. What is the best fix?
options: Keep all four tools and log every call to `issue_refund` and `delete_user_account`
Keep all four tools but require a confirmation prompt before the two risky ones run
Remove `issue_refund` and `delete_user_account` from the agent's configuration
Move to a more capable model that is less likely to call the wrong tool
correct_answer: Remove `issue_refund` and `delete_user_account` from the agent's configuration
explanation: Least privilege means removing capabilities the role does not need (C), which eliminates the attack surface and also cuts token cost. Logging (A) is a detective control that only helps after damage occurs. A confirmation prompt (B) is a compensating control that leaves the capability exposed to prompt injection. A larger model (D) does not change what the agent is authorized to do.

text: A multi-tenant platform uses one shared API key with access to every tenant's documents. Tenant isolation is enforced only by a system prompt line: "Only access documents for the current tenant." What is the critical gap?
options: Tenant isolation relies on a prompt instead of being enforced at the data layer
The shared API key is not rotated often enough to limit the damage of a leak
The isolation instruction should be repeated at the end of the system prompt
The agent should log which tenant's documents it reads on every request
correct_answer: Tenant isolation relies on a prompt instead of being enforced at the data layer
explanation: A prompt is not a security boundary: injection or a simple model error can cross tenants. Isolation must be enforced where the data is accessed (A), using the caller's identity, scoped tokens, and row-level filters. Key rotation (B) is good hygiene but does not add per-tenant access control. Repeating the instruction (C) is still a prompt. Logging (D) is detective and only shows the leak after it happens.

text: Four internal applications and the engineers using Claude Code all need the same Jira and ServiceNow actions. Which connection approach fits best?
options: A direct API wrapper for Jira and ServiceNow, built into each of the applications
An A2A agent that the other applications delegate their Jira and ServiceNow work to
A shared document listing the API endpoints, pasted into each system prompt
An MCP server for Jira and ServiceNow, built once and shared by every client
correct_answer: An MCP server for Jira and ServiceNow, built once and shared by every client
explanation: When the same tools must be reused across several applications and Claude Code, one MCP server maintained once is the fit (D). Direct wrappers (A) duplicate the same integration in every app. A2A (B) adds a whole agent where only tools are needed; it connects agents to agents. Pasting endpoint documentation into prompts (C) gives Claude no way to call the APIs.

text: Managers ask an assistant questions like "How many P1 incidents did EMEA have in Q3?" The answers come from a RAG index over incident reports and are often wrong. Which retrieval strategy fits this query pattern?
options: Increase top-K so the model sees more incident reports for each question
Give Claude a parameterized SQL tool over the incident database
Re-chunk the incident reports into smaller pieces with more overlap
Add BM25 lexical search alongside the existing vector search
correct_answer: Give Claude a parameterized SQL tool over the incident database
explanation: Counting and aggregating is an exact operation: chunks cannot count or join, so expose a parameterized SQL tool (B). More chunks (A) still leave Claude counting from partial samples. Different chunking (C) and hybrid search (D) improve finding the right passages, but no passage contains the total.

text: An agent is connected to several MCP servers with 300 tools in total. Each task uses only a few of them, but every request carries all 300 definitions. The catalog must stay available. What is the best fix?
options: Combine the 300 tools into one general tool that accepts an action name
Shorten every tool description to one line so the definitions use fewer tokens
Mark the tools with `defer_loading` so Claude searches for the ones it needs
Enable prompt caching so the 300 tool definitions cost less on repeated requests
correct_answer: Mark the tools with `defer_loading` so Claude searches for the ones it needs
explanation: When a large catalog must stay available, tool search with `defer_loading` (C) loads only the definitions each task needs, which cuts tokens and tool-selection errors. One catch-all tool (A) hides the schemas Claude needs to call actions correctly. Shorter descriptions (B) make selection harder. Caching (D) lowers the cost of the definitions but leaves all 300 in front of the model to choose between.
